ego.name: Joseph Brant
ego.summary: Joseph Brant, also known by his Mohawk name Thayendanegea, was a Mohawk military and political leader during the American Revolution. Allied with Great Britain, he led Mohawk and Loyalist forces on the New York frontier and, after the war, helped establish the Six Nations community on Ontario's Grand River while advocating for Haudenosaunee interests.

connections.relationship_description: Brant's mother, Margaret Owandah, returned to New York with Joseph and Molly after Peter's death. She married Brant Kanagaraduncka in 1753.
connections.notes: Her Wolf Clan determined Brant's clan identity in matrilineal Mohawk society.

connections.relationship_description: Mohawk sachem who married Brant's mother in 1753. His Canajoharie household had close ties to William Johnson.
connections.notes: His surname was adopted by Joseph and Molly Brant.

connections.relationship_description: Brant's older sister and a Mohawk leader. Her partnership with William Johnson connected Joseph Brant to British imperial officials.
connections.notes: Some accounts allow that they may have been maternal half-siblings, but Mohawk society regarded them as full siblings because they shared a mother.

connections.relationship_description: Brant's wife and a Mohawk clan mother. They married at Niagara in the winter of 1779–1780 and raised their family in Upper Canada.
connections.notes: Catharine's hereditary authority as a clan mother made the marriage significant within Mohawk political life as well as family life.

connections.relationship_description: Son of Joseph and Catharine Brant. He later pursued recognition of Grand River land rights and became a Mohawk chief and Upper Canadian legislator.
connections.notes: John was still a child when Joseph Brant died in 1807.

connections.relationship_description: British Superintendent of Indian Affairs who supported Brant's education and introduced him to colonial leaders. Johnson was also Molly Brant's partner.
connections.notes: Johnson was also the common-law husband of Brant's sister Molly.

connections.relationship_description: British Indian Department official who worked with Brant and traveled with him to London in 1775. Their mission sought British commitments on Haudenosaunee land and alliance.
connections.notes: Guy Johnson succeeded William Johnson as superintendent in 1774.

connections.relationship_description: Brant and Sir John Johnson jointly commanded British-allied Mohawk and Loyalist forces in the 1777 Battle of Oriskany.
connections.notes: Their wartime cooperation tied Brant closely to the Loyalist Johnson network.

connections.relationship_description: Brant's protégé at Grand River in the 1790s. Norton learned Mohawk language and culture under Brant's guidance.
connections.notes: Norton was adopted into a Mohawk family and treated Brant as an adoptive uncle.

connections.relationship_description: Governor of Quebec who issued the 1784 proclamation granting Grand River land to Brant and other Haudenosaunee allies displaced from New York.
connections.notes: The grant became the territorial basis for the Six Nations community on the Grand River.

connections.relationship_description: Founder of Moor's Indian Charity School, where Brant studied from 1761 to 1763. Wheelock provided Brant with English-language and religious education.
connections.notes: Wheelock described Brant as intelligent, courteous, and benevolent.

connections.relationship_description: Brant's father was a Christian Mohawk recorded in Anglican Church records at Fort Hunter; he died while Brant was young.
connections.notes: His early death preceded the family's return from the Ohio Country to the Mohawk Valley.

connections.relationship_description: As a British Indian Department official and Loyalist commander, Butler worked in the same frontier war system as Brant; their forces fought together at the Battle of Newtown in 1779.
connections.notes: At Newtown, Brant and Butler favored mobile harassment of the Continental Army rather than a fixed stand.

connections.relationship_description: Fellow Mohawk war chief who worked with Brant on postwar resettlement and land claims. Deseronto settled at the Bay of Quinte, while Brant chose the Grand River.
connections.notes: They differed over postwar settlement: Deseronto chose the Bay of Quinte, while Brant chose the Grand River.

connections.relationship_description: British king whom Brant met in London during the 1775–1776 diplomatic journey. Brant sought protection for Haudenosaunee land rights and support for an alliance with the Crown.
connections.notes: The meeting placed Brant among the few Indigenous leaders to conduct diplomacy directly at the British court.

connections.relationship_description: Brant and Washington met, but they stood on opposing sides of the American Revolution; Washington ordered the 1779 Sullivan Expedition against British-allied Haudenosaunee communities that Brant defended.
connections.notes: The campaign devastated Haudenosaunee towns and intensified the displacement that shaped Brant's postwar diplomacy.

connections.relationship_description: Anglican clergyman at Fort Hunter who worked with Brant as an interpreter, Mohawk-language teacher, and translator of Christian texts.
connections.notes: This work used Brant's bilingual skills in service of Anglican religious instruction.

connections.relationship_description: Fellow student Brant met at Moor's Indian Charity School. Kirkland later worked as a missionary in western New York.
connections.notes: The available extract documents their contact at school but does not describe a sustained later relationship.

category_summaries.summary: Brant's family rooted him in the matrilineal Mohawk world and connected him to British colonial society. Margaret and Brant Kanagaraduncka established the Canajoharie household where he grew up. Molly Brant's partnership with William Johnson brought him into influential diplomatic circles. His marriage to Catharine joined him to a clan mother, and their son John later continued Grand River land advocacy.

Brant's professional circle linked Mohawk leadership with the British Indian Department and Loyalist military command. William Johnson gave him education and access to colonial officials. Guy Johnson, Sir John Johnson, and John Butler worked with him during the frontier war. At Grand River, Brant mentored John Norton while pursuing a future for displaced Haudenosaunee communities.

Brant used diplomacy with British leaders to seek security for Mohawk and wider Haudenosaunee interests. His London audience with George III sought protection for Indigenous land during the Revolution. Haldimand's 1784 Grand River grant enabled postwar resettlement. Washington's Sullivan campaign destroyed many British-allied Haudenosaunee settlements and deepened the displacement Brant addressed after the war.

Moor's Indian Charity School gave Brant English literacy and familiarity with colonial religious life. Wheelock's instruction and his meeting with Samuel Kirkland prepared him for later work as a translator and diplomat.
